danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 29
paragraphs: Da den franske officer gik ind i værelset med Pierre, følte sidstnævnte det atter som sin pligt at forsikre ham om, at han ikke var franskmand og ønskede at gå, men officeren ville ikke høre tale om det. Han var så overordentlig høflig, elskværdig, godmodig og oprigtigt taknemmelig over for Pierre for at have reddet hans liv, at Pierre ikke kunne nænne at afslå og satte sig ned med ham i stuen — det første værelse, de kom ind i. Over for Pierres forsikringer om, at han ikke var franskmand, trak kaptajnen, der tydeligvis ikke forstod, hvordan nogen kunne afvise en så smigrende betegnelse, på skuldrene og sagde, at hvis Pierre absolut insisterede på at udgive sig for russer, lad det så være, men at han desuagtet for altid ville være bundet til Pierre i taknemmelighed for at have reddet hans liv.

Havde denne mand haft den mindste evne til at opfatte andres følelser og havde han overhovedet forstået, hvad Pierre følte, ville sidstnævnte sandsynligvis have forladt ham, men mandens livlige uimodtagelighed for alt andet end sig selv afvæbnede Pierre.

»Franskmand eller russisk fyrste inkognito,« sagde officeren og kiggede på Pierres fine, om end snavsede linned og ringen på hans finger. »Jeg skylder Dem mit liv og tilbyder Dem mit venskab. En franskmand glemmer aldrig hverken en fornærmelse eller en tjeneste. Jeg tilbyder Dem mit venskab. Det er alt, hvad jeg kan sige.«

Der var så megen godmodighed og ædelhed (i ordets franske forstand) i officerens stemme, i hans ansigtsudtryk og gestus, at Pierre, ubevidst smilende som svar på franskmandens smil, trykkede den fremrakte hånd.

»Kaptajn Ramballe, af det 13. lette regiment, ridder af Æreslegionen for begivenheden den syvende september,« præsenterede han sig, idet et selvtilfreds, utilbagehold smil krusede hans læber under overskægget. »Vil De nu være så venlig at fortælle mig, med hvem jeg har den ære at samtale så behageligt, i stedet for at ligge på lazarettet med den galnings kugle i kroppen?«
Pierre svarede, at han ikke kunne opgive sit navn, og begyndte rødmende at forsøge at finde på et navn og sige noget om sin grund til at skjule det, men franskmanden afbrød ham hastigt.

»Åh, jeg forstår!« sagde han. »De er officer... en højere officer måske. De har båret våben mod os. Det er ikke min sag. Jeg skylder Dem mit liv. Det er nok for mig. Jeg er helt til Deres tjeneste. De tilhører adelen?« sluttede han med et spørgende strejf i sin tone. Pierre bøjede hovedet. »Deres fornavn, om jeg må bede. Det er alt, hvad jeg ønsker at vide. Monsieur Pierre, siger De... Udmærket.«

Da lammekøllen og en omelet var blevet serveret og en samovar og vodka bragt ind tillige med noget vin, som franskmændene havde taget fra en russisk kælder og medbragt, inviterede Ramballe Pierre til at dele hans middag og begyndte selv at spise grådigt og hurtigt som en sund og sulten mand, tyggede sin mad hurtigt med sine stærke tænder, uophørligt smaskede og gentog: »Udmærket! Lækkert!« Hans ansigt blev rødt og dækkedes af sved. Pierre var sulten og delte med glæde måltidet. Morel, oppasseren, bragte noget varmt vand i en kasserolle og stillede en flaske rødvin i det. Han bragte også en flaske kvas, taget fra køkkenet, som de kunne prøve. Den drik var allerede kendt af franskmændene og havde fået et særligt navn. De kaldte den limonade de cochon (svinelemonade), og Morel talte godt om den limonade de cochon, han havde fundet i køkkenet. Men da kaptajnen havde vinen, de havde taget under passagen gennem Moskva, overlod han kvasen til Morel og tog fat på flasken bordeaux. Han svøbte flasken op til halsen i en serviet og skænkede vin til sig selv og Pierre. Tilfredsstillelsen af hans sult og vinen gjorde kaptajnen endnu mere livlig, og han snakkede uafbrudt under hele middagen.

»Ja, min kære monsieur Pierre, jeg skylder Dem et smukt votivlys for at redde mig fra den galning... De kan se, jeg har kugler nok i kroppen allerede. Her er en, jeg fik ved Wagram« (han rørte ved sin side) »og en anden ved Smolensk« — han viste et ar på kinden — »og dette ben, som De kan se, ikke vil marchere, fik jeg den syvende ved det store slag ved la Moskowa. Sacré Dieu! Det var storslået! Den ildregn var værd at se. Det var et hårdt stykke arbejde, I satte os til, det kan I tro! De kan være stolt af det. Og på min ære, trods den hoste, jeg fik dér, ville jeg være rede til at begynde forfra. Jeg har ondt af dem, der ikke så det.«
»Jeg var der,« sagde Pierre.

»Nej virkelig? Så meget desto bedre! De er sandelig tapre fjender. Den store skanse holdt godt stand, ved min pibe!« fortsatte franskmanden. »Og I lod os betale dyrt for den. Tre gange var jeg deroppe — lige så sikkert som jeg sidder her. Tre gange nåede vi kanonerne, og tre gange blev vi kastet tilbage som papfigurer. Åh, det var smukt, monsieur Pierre! Jeres grenaderer var prægtige, ved himlen! Jeg så dem slutte rækkerne seks gange i træk og marchere som på parade. Fine karle! Vores konge af Napoli, der forstår den slags, råbte 'Bravo!' Ha, ha! Så De er en af os soldater!« tilføjede han smilende efter et øjebliks pause. »Så meget desto bedre, monsieur Pierre! Forfærdelig i kamp... galant... over for det smukke køn« (han blinkede og smilede), »det er franskmændene, monsieur Pierre, er det ikke?«

Kaptajnen var så naivt og godmodigt munter, så ægte og så tilfreds med sig selv, at Pierre næsten blinkede tilbage, mens han kiggede fornøjet på ham. Sandsynligvis rettede ordet »galant« kaptajnens tanker mod tilstanden i Moskva.
»Apropros, sig mig, er det virkelig sandt, at alle kvinderne har forladt Moskva? Sikken besynderlig idé! Hvad havde de at frygte?«
»Ville de franske damer ikke forlade Paris, hvis russerne rykkede ind?« spurgte Pierre.
»Ha, ha, ha!« Franskmanden udstødte en munter, sangvinsk latter og klappede Pierre på skulderen. »Sikke noget at sige!« udbrød han. »Paris?... Men Paris, Paris...«
»Paris — verdens hovedstad,« fuldførte Pierre hans bemærkning.
Kaptajnen kiggede på Pierre. Han havde den vane at standse midt i sin tale og stirre indgående med sine leende, venlige øjne.

»Nå, hvis De ikke havde fortalt mig, at De var russer, ville jeg have væddet på, at De var pariser! De har det... det ved jeg ikke hvad, det...« Og efter at have udtalt dette kompliment kiggede han igen tavst på ham.
»Jeg har været i Paris. Jeg tilbragte årevis der,« sagde Pierre.

»Åh ja, det kan man tydeligt se. Paris!... En mand, der ikke kender Paris, er en vildmand. Man kan kende en pariser på to mils afstand. Paris er Talma, la Duchénois, Potier, Sorbonne, boulevarderne,« og da han bemærkede, at hans konklusion var svagere end det foregående, tilføjede han hurtigt: »Der er kun ét Paris i verden. De har været i Paris og er forblevet russer. Nå, jeg agter Dem ikke desto mindre for det.«
Under indflydelse af den vin, han havde drukket, og efter de dage, han havde tilbragt alene med sine triste tanker, nød Pierre uvilkårligt samtalen med denne muntre og godmodige mand.

»For at vende tilbage til Deres damer — jeg hører, de er dejlige. Sikken ynkelig idé at gå hen og begrave sig ude på steppen, når den franske hær er i Moskva. Sikken chance de piger har forspildt! Jeres bønder — det er en anden sag; men I civiliserede folk burde kende os bedre. Vi tog Wien, Berlin, Madrid, Napoli, Rom, Warszawa, alle verdens hovedstæder... Man frygter os, men man holder af os. Vi er rare at lære at kende. Og så kejseren...« begyndte han, men Pierre afbrød ham.
»Kejseren,« gentog Pierre, og hans ansigt blev pludselig trist og forlegen, »er kejseren...?«

»Kejseren? Han er gavmildhed, barmhjertighed, retfærdighed, orden, geni — det er, hvad kejseren er! Det er mig, Ramballe, der siger det... Jeg forsikrer Dem, for otte år siden var jeg hans fjende. Min far var en emigrantgreve... Men den mand har besejret mig. Han har grebet fat i mig. Jeg kunne ikke modstå synet af den storhed og herlighed, han har dækket Frankrig med. Da jeg forstod, hvad han ville — da jeg så, at han redte et leje af laurbær for os, sagde jeg til mig selv: 'Det er en monark,' og jeg viede mig til ham! Så det! Åh ja, mon cher, han er den største mand i alle tiders fortid og fremtid.«
»Er han i Moskva?« stammede Pierre med et skyldigt blik.
Franskmanden kiggede på hans skyldige ansigt og smilede.
»Nej, han gør sit indtog i morgen,« svarede han og fortsatte sin snak.

Deres samtale blev afbrudt af råb fra adskillige stemmer ved porten og af Morel, der kom for at sige, at nogle württembergske husarer var kommet og ville stalde deres heste i gården, hvor kaptajnens heste stod. Denne vanskelighed var hovedsageligt opstået, fordi husarerne ikke forstod, hvad der blev sagt til dem på fransk.

Kaptajnen lod deres oversergeant kalde ind og spurgte ham med streng stemme, hvilket regiment han tilhørte, hvem hans chef var, og med hvilken ret han tillod sig at lægge beslag på kvarterer, der allerede var besatte. Tyskeren, der kunne lidt fransk, besvarede de to første spørgsmål ved at nævne sit regiment og sin chef, men på det tredje spørgsmål, som han ikke forstod, svarede han med at blande brudt fransk ind i sit tysk og forklare, at han var regimentets kvartermester, og at hans chef havde befalet ham at besætte alle husene ét efter ét. Pierre, der kunne tysk, oversatte, hvad tyskeren sagde, for kaptajnen og gav kaptajnens svar til den württembergske husar på tysk. Da tyskeren forstod, hvad der blev sagt, føjede han sig og førte sine mænd andetsteds hen. Kaptajnen gik ud på trappen og gav nogle ordrer med høj stemme.

Da han vendte tilbage til værelset, sad Pierre på samme sted som før med hovedet i hænderne. Hans ansigt udtrykte lidelse. Han led virkelig i det øjeblik. Da kaptajnen var gået ud, og han var alene, var han pludselig kommet til sig selv og havde indset den situation, han befandt sig i. Det var ikke det, at Moskva var taget, eller at de lykkelige sejrherrer var herrer i den og nedlod sig til ham. Hvor smertefuldt det end var, var det ikke det, der plagede Pierre i øjeblikket. Han var plaget af bevidstheden om sin egen svaghed. De få glas vin, han havde drukket, og samtalen med denne godmodige mand havde ødelagt den stemning af koncentreret dysterhed, hvori han havde tilbragt de seneste dage, og som var afgørende for gennemførelsen af hans plan. Pistolen, dolken og bondefrakken lå klar. Napoleon ville rykke ind i byen næste dag. Pierre anså det stadig for nyttigt og værdigt at dræbe den onde; men nu følte han, at han ikke ville gøre det. Han vidste ikke hvorfor, men han anede, at han ikke ville gennemføre sin hensigt. Han kæmpede mod tilståelsen af sin svaghed, men fornam dunkelt, at han ikke kunne overvinde den, og at hans tidligere dystre sindsstemning med tanker om hævn, drab og selvopofrelse var blevet spredt som støv ved kontakten med det første menneske, han mødte.
Kaptajnen vendte tilbage til værelset, let haltende og fløjtende en melodi.

Franskmandens snak, der tidligere havde moret Pierre, frastødte ham nu. Den melodi, han fløjtede, hans gang og den gestus, hvormed han snoede sit overskæg, virkede nu anstødelige. »Jeg går straks. Jeg siger ikke et ord mere til ham,« tænkte Pierre. Det tænkte han, men alligevel blev han siddende på samme sted. En mærkelig følelse af svaghed bandt ham til stedet; han ønskede at rejse sig og gå, men kunne ikke.
Kaptajnen derimod virkede meget oplagt. Han gik frem og tilbage i værelset to gange. Hans øjne skinnede, og hans overskæg dirrede, som om han smilede for sig selv af en morsom tanke.
»Württembergernes oberst er henrivende,« sagde han pludselig. »Han er tysker, men en flink fyr alligevel... Men han er tysker.« Han satte sig over for Pierre. »I øvrigt kan De altså tysk?«
Pierre kiggede tavst på ham.
»Hvad hedder 'husly' på tysk?«
»Husly?« gentog Pierre. »Husly hedder på tysk Unterkunft.«
»Hvad siger De?« spurgte kaptajnen hurtigt og tvivlende.
»Unterkunft,« gentog Pierre.
»Onterkoff,« sagde kaptajnen og kiggede på Pierre i nogle sekunder med leende øjne. »De tyskere er helt håbløse tåber, synes De ikke, monsieur Pierre?« konkluderede han.
»Nå, lad os tage endnu en flaske af denne moskva-bordeaux, hva? Morel varmer endnu en lille flaske til os. Morel!« råbte han muntert.

Morel bragte stearinlys og en flaske vin. Kaptajnen kiggede på Pierre i stearinlysenes skær og blev tydeligvis slået af det forpinte udtryk i sin ledsagers ansigt. Ramballe nærmede sig Pierre med oprigtig bekymring og medfølelse i ansigtet og bøjede sig over ham.
»Se nu, vi er kede af det,« sagde han og berørte Pierres hånd. »Har jeg forstyrret Dem? Nej, virkelig, har De noget imod mig?« spurgte han Pierre. »Måske er det situationen?«
Pierre svarede ikke, men kiggede hjerteligt ind i franskmandens øjne, hvis udtryk af medfølelse behagede ham.

»Ærligt talt, ud over hvad jeg skylder Dem, føler jeg venskab for Dem. Kan jeg gøre noget for Dem? Disponér over mig. Det gælder på liv og død. Jeg siger det med hånden på hjertet!« sagde han og slog sig for brystet.
»Tak,« sagde Pierre.
Kaptajnen kiggede indgående på ham, ligesom da han erfarede, at »husly« hedder Unterkunft på tysk, og hans ansigt opklaredes pludselig.
»Nå, i det tilfælde drikker jeg på vores venskab!« udbrød han muntert og fyldte to glas med vin.
Pierre tog det ene glas og tømte det. Ramballe tømte også sit, trykkede igen Pierres hånd og lænede sig med albuerne på bordet i en eftertænksom stilling.

»Ja, min kære ven,« begyndte han, »sådan er skæbnens luner. Hvem ville have sagt, at jeg skulle blive soldat og dragonkaptajn i Bonapartes tjeneste, som vi plejede at kalde ham? Og dog er jeg her i Moskva med ham. Jeg må fortælle Dem, mon cher,« fortsatte han i den triste og afmålte tone hos en mand, der agter at fortælle en lang historie, »at vores navn er et af de ældste i Frankrig.«

Og med en franskmands lette og naive åbenhjertighed fortalte kaptajnen Pierre historien om sine forfædre, sin barndom, ungdom og manddom og alt om sine slægtninge og sin økonomiske og familiemæssige situation, idet ma pauvre mère naturligvis spillede en vigtig rolle i fortællingen.
»Men alt det er bare livets ramme; det virkelige er kærligheden — kærlighed! Har jeg ikke ret, monsieur Pierre?« sagde han og blev ivrig. »Endnu et glas?«
Pierre tømte igen sit glas og skænkede sig et tredje.
»Åh, kvinder, kvinder!« Og kaptajnen kiggede på Pierre med glitrende øjne og begyndte at tale om kærlighed og sine kærlighedshistorier.

Der var rigtig mange af dem, og det kunne man let tro, når man kiggede på officerens flotte, selvtilfredse ansigt og noterede den ivrige entusiasme, hvormed han talte om kvinder. Selvom alle Ramballes kærlighedshistorier havde den sanselige karakter, som franskmænd betragter som den særlige charme og poesi i kærlighed, fortalte han sine historier med en så oprigtig overbevisning om, at han alene havde oplevet og kendt al kærlighedens charme, og han beskrev kvinderne så tillokkende, at Pierre lyttede til ham med nysgerrighed.

Det var tydeligt, at den l'amour, franskmanden var så glad for, hverken var den lave og simple slags, Pierre engang havde følt for sin kone, eller den romantiske kærlighed, han havde oparbejdet i sig selv over for Natasja. (Ramballe foragtede begge disse former for kærlighed lige meget: den ene kaldte han »bønderkærlighed« og den anden »tåbekærlighed.«) Den l'amour, franskmanden dyrkede, bestod hovedsageligt i det unaturlige i hans forhold til kvinden og i en kombination af modsigelser, der gav følelsen dens vigtigste charme.

Således genfortalte kaptajnen rørende historien om sin kærlighed til en fascinerende marquise på femogtredive og samtidig til et charmerende, uskyldigt barn på sytten, marquise'ens datter. Konflikten i storsindethed mellem moderen og datteren, der endte med moderens opofrelse af sig selv og tilbud om sin datter i ægteskab til sin elsker, rørte stadig kaptajnen, skønt det var mindet om en fjern fortid. Derefter genfortalte han en episode, hvor ægtemanden spillede elskerens rolle, og han — elskeren — påtog sig ægtemandens rolle, samt adskillige morsomme hændelser fra sine minder om Tyskland, hvor »husly« hedder Unterkunft, og mændene spiser surkål, og de unge piger er »for blonde.«

Endelig var den seneste episode i Polen, der stadig var frisk i kaptajnens erindring, og som han fortalte med hurtige gestus og glødende ansigt, om, hvordan han havde reddet en polaks liv (i det hele taget optrådte livredderi ustandseligt i kaptajnens historier), og polakken havde betroet ham sin fortryllende hustru (parisienne de cœur), mens han selv trådte i fransk tjeneste. Kaptajnen var lykkelig, den bedårende polske dame ønskede at flygte med ham, men tilskyndet af storsind førte kaptajnen hustruen tilbage til ægtemanden, idet han sagde: »Jeg har reddet Deres liv, og jeg redder Deres ære!« Efter at have gentaget disse ord tørrede kaptajnen sine øjne og rystede sig, som for at fordrive den svaghed, der overvældede ham ved denne rørende erindring.

Mens Pierre lyttede til kaptajnens fortællinger, fulgte han — som det ofte sker sent om aftenen og under vinens indflydelse — alt, hvad der blev fortalt, forstod det alt sammen, og fulgte samtidig et spor af personlige erindringer, der, han vidste ikke hvorfor, pludselig steg op i hans sind. Mens han lyttede til disse kærlighedshistorier, rejste hans egen kærlighed til Natasja sig uventet i hans tanker, og idet han gennemgik billederne af den kærlighed i sin fantasi, sammenlignede han dem mentalt med Ramballes fortællinger. Da han lyttede til historien om kampen mellem kærlighed og pligt, så Pierre for sine øjne enhver mindste detalje af sit sidste møde med genstanden for sin kærlighed ved Sukharev-vandtårnet. Dengang havde dette møde ikke gjort indtryk på ham — han havde ikke tænkt på det en eneste gang. Men nu forekom det ham, at det møde rummede noget meget vigtigt og poetisk.

»Pjotr Kirillovitj, kom herhen! Vi har genkendt Dem,« syntes han nu at høre de ord, hun havde sagt, og at se for sig hendes øjne, hendes smil, hendes rejsekyse og en løs hårlok... og der var noget gribende og rørende i alt dette.

Da franskmanden var færdig med sin historie om den bedårende polske dame, spurgte kaptajnen Pierre, om han nogensinde havde oplevet en lignende drift til at ofre sig for kærligheden og en følelse af misundelse over for den retmæssige ægtemand.

Udfordret af dette spørgsmål løftede Pierre hovedet og følte et behov for at udtrykke de tanker, der fyldte hans sind. Han begyndte at forklare, at han opfattede kærligheden til en kvinde noget anderledes. Han sagde, at han i hele sit liv havde elsket og stadig elskede kun én kvinde, og at hun aldrig kunne blive hans.
»Tiens!« sagde kaptajnen.

Pierre forklarede derefter, at han havde elsket denne kvinde fra sine tidligste år, men at han ikke havde vovet at tænke på hende, fordi hun var for ung, og fordi han havde været en uægte søn uden navn. Senere, da han havde fået et navn og rigdom, vovede han ikke at tænke på hende, fordi han elskede hende for højt og stillede hende langt over alt i verden og især derfor over sig selv.
Da Pierre var nået hertil, spurgte han kaptajnen, om han forstod det.
Kaptajnen gjorde en gestus, der antydede, at selv om han ikke forstod det, bad han Pierre om at fortsætte.
»Platonisk kærlighed, skyer...« mumlede han.

Enten var det den vin, han havde drukket, eller en drift mod åbenhjertighed, eller tanken om, at denne mand ikke kendte og aldrig ville kende nogen af dem, der spillede en rolle i hans historie, eller måske var det alt dette tilsammen — noget løste Pierres tunge. Med tyk stemme og et fjernt blik i sine skinnende øjne fortalte han hele historien om sit liv: sit ægteskab, Natasjas kærlighed til hans bedste ven, hendes svigt af ham, og alle hans egne enkle forbindelser til hende. Tilskyndet af Ramballes spørgsmål fortalte han også, hvad han i begyndelsen havde holdt skjult — sin egen stilling og endda sit navn.

Mere end noget andet i Pierres historie var kaptajnen imponeret over, at Pierre var meget rig, havde to palæer i Moskva, og at han havde opgivet alt og ikke forladt byen, men var forblevet dér og skjulte sit navn og sin stand.

Da det var sent om natten, gik de ud sammen på gaden. Natten var varm og lys. Til venstre for huset på Pokrovka glødede en ild — den første af dem, der begyndte i Moskva. Til højre og højt oppe på himlen stod den aftagende halvmånes segl, og over for den hang den klare komet, der i Pierres hjerte var forbundet med hans kærlighed. Ved porten stod Gerasim, kokken og to franskmænd. Deres latter og deres gensidigt uforståelige bemærkninger på to sprog kunne høres. De kiggede på det skær, der sås i byen.
Der var intet forfærdeligt i den ene lille, fjerne ild i den uhyre by.

Med blikket rettet mod den høje, stjerneklare himmel, mod månen, mod kometen og mod ildens skær oplevede Pierre en glædesfuld følelse. »Se nu, hvor godt det er; hvad mere behøver man?« tænkte han. Og pludselig, da han huskede sin hensigt, blev han svimmel og følte sig så mat, at han måtte støtte sig mod hegnet for ikke at falde.
Uden at tage afsked med sin nye ven forlod Pierre porten med usikre skridt og vendte tilbage til sit værelse, lagde sig på sofaen og faldt straks i søvn.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 29
paragraphs: When the French officer went into the room with Pierre, the latter again thought it his duty to assure him that he was not French and wished to leave, but the officer would not hear of it. He was so polite, friendly, good-natured, and genuinely grateful to Pierre for saving his life that Pierre couldn't bring himself to refuse, and sat down with him in the parlor—the first room they entered. To Pierre's insistence that he was not a Frenchman, the captain, evidently unable to understand how anyone could decline so flattering a designation, shrugged his shoulders and said that if Pierre absolutely insisted on passing for a Russian, so be it, but that he would be forever bound to Pierre by gratitude for saving his life.

Had this man been capable of even slightly perceiving the feelings of others, and had he at all understood what Pierre's feelings were, Pierre would probably have left him. But the man's oblivious self-absorption disarmed Pierre.

"A Frenchman or a Russian prince incognito," said the officer, looking at Pierre's fine though dirty linen and at the ring on his finger. "I owe my life to you and offer you my friendship. A Frenchman never forgets either an insult or a service. I offer you my friendship. That is all I can say."

There was so much good nature and nobility (in the French sense of the word) in the officer's voice, in the expression of his face, and in his gestures, that Pierre, unconsciously smiling in response to the Frenchman's smile, shook the hand held out to him.

"Captain Ramballe, of the 13th Light Regiment, Chevalier of the Legion of Honor for the affair on the seventh of September," he introduced himself, a self-satisfied, irrepressible smile puckering his lips under his mustache. "Will you now be so good as to tell me with whom I have the honor of conversing so pleasantly, instead of being in the field hospital with that maniac's bullet in my body?"
Pierre replied that he could not tell him his name and, blushing, began to try to invent a name and explain his reason for concealing it, but the Frenchman hastily interrupted him.

"Oh, please!" said he. "I understand your reasons. You are an officer... a superior officer perhaps. You have borne arms against us. That's not my business. I owe you my life. That is enough for me. I am entirely at your service. You belong to the gentry?" he concluded with a shade of inquiry in his tone. Pierre bent his head. "Your first name, if you please. That is all I ask. Monsieur Pierre, you say?... That's all I want to know."

When the mutton and an omelet had been served and a samovar and vodka brought, along with some wine which the French had taken from a Russian cellar, Ramballe invited Pierre to share his dinner and immediately began eating greedily and quickly like a healthy, hungry man, chewing his food rapidly with his strong teeth, continually smacking his lips and repeating: "Excellent! Delicious!" His face grew red and was covered with sweat. Pierre was hungry and shared the dinner with pleasure. Morel, the orderly, brought some hot water in a saucepan and placed a bottle of claret in it. He also brought a bottle of kvass from the kitchen for them to try. That drink was already known to the French and had been given a special name. They called it "pig's lemonade," and Morel spoke well of the pig's lemonade he had found in the kitchen. But since the captain had the wine they had taken while passing through Moscow, he left the kvass to Morel and turned to the bottle of Bordeaux. He wrapped the bottle up to its neck in a napkin and poured out wine for himself and for Pierre. The satisfaction of his hunger and the wine made the captain still livelier, and he chatted nonstop all through dinner.

"Yes, my dear Monsieur Pierre, I owe you a fine votive candle for saving me from that maniac... You see, I've got enough bullets in my body already. Here is one I got at Wagram" (he touched his side) "and a second at Smolensk"—he showed a scar on his cheek—"and this leg which as you see doesn't want to cooperate, I got that on the seventh at the great battle of la Moskowa. Good Lord! It was splendid! That storm of fire was worth seeing. It was a tough job you set us there, I must say! You may be proud of it! And on my honor, despite the cough I caught there, I'd be ready to do it all over again. I pity those who missed it."
"I was there," said Pierre.

"Really? So much the better! You are certainly brave enemies. The great redoubt held out well, by my word!" continued the Frenchman. "And you made us pay dearly for it. I was at it three times—I swear it. Three times we reached the guns and three times we were thrown back like cardboard figures. Oh, it was magnificent, Monsieur Pierre! Your grenadiers were superb, by heaven! I saw them close up their ranks six times in a row and march as if on parade. Wonderful men! Our King of Naples, who knows what's what, cried 'Bravo!' Ha, ha! So you are one of us soldiers!" he added, smiling, after a momentary pause. "So much the better, so much the better, Monsieur Pierre! Terrible in battle... gallant with the ladies" (he winked and smiled), "that's what the French are, Monsieur Pierre, isn't it?"

The captain was so naturally and good-humoredly cheerful, so genuine, and so pleased with himself that Pierre almost winked back as he looked merrily at him. Probably the word "gallant" turned the captain's thoughts to the state of Moscow.
"By the way, tell me, is it true that the women have all left Moscow? What a strange idea! What did they have to be afraid of?"
"Would not the French ladies leave Paris if the Russians entered it?" asked Pierre.
"Ha, ha, ha!" The Frenchman let out a merry, hearty chuckle, patting Pierre on the shoulder. "What a thing to say!" he exclaimed. "Paris?... But Paris, Paris..."
"Paris—the capital of the world," Pierre finished for him.
The captain looked at Pierre. He had a habit of stopping short in the middle of his talk and gazing intently with his laughing, kindly eyes.
"Well, if you hadn't told me you were Russian, I would have bet you were Parisian! You have that certain something, that..." and having paid this compliment, he again gazed at Pierre in silence.
"I have been in Paris. I spent years there," said Pierre.

"Oh yes, one can tell. Paris! A man who doesn't know Paris is a savage. You can spot a Parisian two leagues away. Paris is Talma, la Duchenois, Potier, the Sorbonne, the boulevards," and noticing that his conclusion was weaker than what had come before, he added quickly: "There is only one Paris in the world. You have been to Paris and have remained Russian. Well, I don't think any less of you for it."
Under the influence of the wine and after the days spent alone with his depressing thoughts, Pierre involuntarily enjoyed talking with this cheerful, good-natured man.

"To return to your ladies—I hear they are beautiful. What a foolish idea to go bury themselves in the steppes when the French army is in Moscow. What a chance those girls have missed! Your peasants—that's another matter; but you civilized people ought to know us better. We took Vienna, Berlin, Madrid, Naples, Rome, Warsaw—all the world's capitals. We are feared, but we are loved. We are good to know. And then the Emperor..." he began, but Pierre interrupted him.
"The Emperor," Pierre repeated, and his face suddenly became sad and embarrassed. "Is the Emperor...?"

"The Emperor? He is generosity, mercy, justice, order, genius—that's what the Emperor is! It is I, Ramballe, who tell you so... I assure you I was his enemy eight years ago. My father was an emigrant count... But that man has won me over. He seized hold of me. I could not resist the sight of the grandeur and glory with which he has covered France. When I understood what he wanted—when I saw that he was preparing a bed of laurels for us—I said to myself: 'That is a monarch,' and I devoted myself to him! And so there it is! Oh yes, my dear friend, he is the greatest man of the ages past or future."
"Is he in Moscow?" Pierre asked with a guilty look.
The Frenchman looked at his guilty face and smiled.
"No, he will make his entry tomorrow," he replied, and continued his talk.

Their conversation was interrupted by cries of several voices at the gate and by Morel, who came to say that some Wurttemberg hussars had arrived and wanted to put their horses in the yard where the captain's horses were. This difficulty had arisen mainly because the hussars did not understand what was being said to them in French.

The captain had their senior sergeant called in and in a stern voice asked him what regiment he belonged to, who his commanding officer was, and by what right he allowed himself to claim quarters that were already occupied. The German, who knew little French, answered the first two questions by giving the names of his regiment and commanding officer, but in reply to the third—which he did not understand—said, mixing broken French into his German, that he was the quartermaster of the regiment and his commander had ordered him to occupy all the houses one after another. Pierre, who knew German, translated what the German said to the captain and gave the captain's reply to the Wurttemberg hussar in German. When the German understood what was being said, he submitted and took his men elsewhere. The captain went out onto the porch and gave some orders in a loud voice.

When he returned to the room, Pierre was sitting in the same place as before, with his head in his hands. His face showed suffering. He really was suffering at that moment. When the captain went out and Pierre was left alone, he suddenly came to his senses and realized the position he was in. It was not that Moscow had been taken or that the happy conquerors were masters in it and patronizing him. Painful as that was, it was not what tormented Pierre. He was tormented by the consciousness of his own weakness. The few glasses of wine he had drunk and the conversation with this good-natured man had destroyed the mood of concentrated gloom in which he had spent the last few days, and which was essential for carrying out his plan. The pistol, dagger, and peasant coat were ready. Napoleon was to enter the city the next day. Pierre still believed it would be useful and worthy to kill the tyrant, but now he felt he would not do it. He did not know why, but sensed that he would not carry out his intention. He struggled against admitting his weakness but dimly felt that he could not overcome it, and that his former dark mood—concerning vengeance, killing, and self-sacrifice—had been scattered like dust by contact with the first man he met.
The captain returned to the room, limping slightly and whistling a tune.

The Frenchman's chatter, which had previously amused Pierre, now repelled him. The tune he was whistling, his walk, and the gesture with which he twirled his mustache all now seemed offensive. "I will leave immediately. I won't say another word to him," thought Pierre. He thought this, but still sat in the same spot. A strange feeling of weakness held him there; he wanted to get up and leave, but could not.
The captain, on the other hand, seemed very cheerful. He paced up and down the room twice. His eyes shone and his mustache twitched as if he were smiling to himself at some amusing thought.

"The colonel of those Wurttembergers is delightful," he suddenly said. "He's a German, but a nice fellow all the same... But he's a German." He sat down facing Pierre. "By the way, you speak German then?"
Pierre looked at him in silence.
"What is the German for 'shelter'?"
"Shelter?" Pierre repeated. "The German for shelter is Unterkunft."
"How do you say it?" the captain asked quickly and doubtfully.
"Unterkunft," Pierre repeated.
"Onterkoff," said the captain, and looked at Pierre for some seconds with laughing eyes. "These Germans are first-rate fools, don't you think so, Monsieur Pierre?" he concluded.
"Well, let's have another bottle of this Moscow Bordeaux, shall we? Morel will warm us up another little bottle. Morel!" he called out cheerfully.

Morel brought candles and a bottle of wine. The captain looked at Pierre by the candlelight and was evidently struck by the troubled expression on his companion's face. Ramballe, with genuine concern and sympathy in his face, went up to Pierre and bent over him.
"Come now, we're sad," said he, touching Pierre's hand. "Have I upset you? No, really, have you anything against me?" he asked. "Perhaps it's the state of affairs?"
Pierre did not answer but looked warmly into the Frenchman's eyes, whose expression of sympathy was pleasing to him.

"Honestly, without speaking of what I owe you, I feel friendship for you. Can I do anything for you? Count on me. It is for life and death. I say it with my hand on my heart!" said he, striking his chest.
"Thank you," said Pierre.
The captain gazed intently at him as he had done when learning that "shelter" was Unterkunft in German, and his face suddenly brightened.
"Well, in that case, I drink to our friendship!" he cried gaily, filling two glasses with wine.
Pierre took one of the glasses and emptied it. Ramballe emptied his too, pressed Pierre's hand again, and leaned his elbows on the table in a pensive attitude.

"Yes, my dear friend," he began, "such are the twists of fortune. Who would have said that I would be a soldier and a captain of dragoons in the service of Bonaparte, as we used to call him? Yet here I am in Moscow with him. I must tell you, my dear friend," he continued in the sad and measured tones of a man who intends to tell a long story, "that our family name is one of the most ancient in France."

And with a Frenchman's easy and natural frankness, the captain told Pierre the story of his ancestors, his childhood, youth, and manhood, and all about his relatives and his financial and family affairs, with "my poor mother" playing of course an important part in the story.
"But all that is only life's setting; the real thing is love—love! Am I not right, Monsieur Pierre?" said he, growing animated. "Another glass?"
Pierre again emptied his glass and poured himself a third.
"Oh, women, women!" and the captain, looking with glistening eyes at Pierre, began talking about love and his love affairs.

There were very many of these, as one could easily believe looking at the officer's handsome, self-satisfied face and noting the eager enthusiasm with which he spoke of women. Though all of Ramballe's love stories had the sensual character which Frenchmen regard as the special charm and poetry of love, he told his story with such sincere conviction that he alone had experienced and known all love's charm, and he described women so enticingly, that Pierre listened to him with curiosity.

It was clear that the kind of love the Frenchman was so fond of was not the low, simple kind that Pierre had once felt for his wife, nor the romantic love, fueled by his own imagination, that he had experienced for Natasha. (Ramballe despised both of these equally: one he called the "love of peasants" and the other the "love of simpletons.") The love the Frenchman worshiped consisted mainly in the artificiality of his relations with women and in a combination of absurdities that gave the feeling its chief appeal.

Thus the captain touchingly recounted the story of his love for a fascinating marquise of thirty-five and at the same time for a charming, innocent child of seventeen—the bewitching marquise's daughter. The conflict of generosity between mother and daughter, ending in the mother sacrificing herself and offering her daughter in marriage to her lover, still moved the captain, though it was a distant memory. Then he recounted an episode in which the husband played the part of the lover and he—the lover—assumed the role of the husband, as well as several amusing incidents from his time in Germany, where "shelter" is called Unterkunft and where the husbands eat sauerkraut and the young girls are "too blonde."

Finally, the most recent episode—in Poland, still fresh in the captain's memory—which he narrated with rapid gestures and a glowing face, was of how he had saved the life of a Pole (in general, the saving of lives continually occurred in the captain's stories) and the Pole had entrusted to him his enchanting wife (a Parisian at heart) while himself entering the French service. The captain was happy, the enchanting Polish lady wished to elope with him, but, prompted by noble feeling, the captain restored the wife to the husband, saying as he did so: "I have saved your life, and I save your honor!" Having repeated these words, the captain wiped his eyes and gave himself a shake, as if driving away the weakness that overcame him at this touching recollection.

Listening to the captain's tales, Pierre—as often happens late in the evening and under the influence of wine—followed all that was told him, understood it all, and at the same time followed a train of personal memories that, he knew not why, suddenly arose in his mind. While listening to these love stories, his own love for Natasha unexpectedly surfaced, and going over the images of that love in his imagination, he mentally compared them with Ramballe's tales. Listening to the story of the struggle between love and duty, Pierre saw before his eyes every tiny detail of his last meeting with the object of his love at the Sukharev water tower. At the time, that meeting had not made an impact on him—he had not even once recalled it. But now it seemed to him that there had been something very important and poetic in it.

"Pyotr Kirilovich, come here! We recognized you," he now seemed to hear the words she had spoken and to see before him her eyes, her smile, her traveling hood, and a stray lock of her hair... and there seemed to him something deeply touching in all of this.

Having finished his tale about the enchanting Polish lady, the captain asked Pierre if he had ever experienced a similar urge to sacrifice himself for love and a feeling of envy of the legitimate husband.

Prompted by this question, Pierre raised his head and felt a need to express the thoughts that filled his mind. He began to explain that he understood love for a woman somewhat differently. He said that in all his life he had loved and still loved only one woman, and that she could never be his.
"Really!" said the captain.

Pierre then explained that he had loved this woman from his earliest years, but had not dared to think of her because she was too young, and because he had been an illegitimate son without a name. Later, when he had received a name and wealth, he dared not think of her because he loved her too much, placing her far above everything in the world, and especially therefore above himself.
When he had reached this point, Pierre asked the captain whether he understood that.
The captain made a gesture suggesting that even if he did not understand it, he begged Pierre to continue.
"Platonic love, clouds..." he muttered.

Whether it was the wine he had drunk, or an impulse of frankness, or the thought that this man did not and never would know any of those who played a part in his story, or whether it was all these things together, something loosened Pierre's tongue. Speaking thickly and with a faraway look in his shining eyes, he told the whole story of his life: his marriage, Natasha's love for his best friend, her betrayal of him, and all his own simple relations with her. Urged on by Ramballe's questions, he also told what he had first kept hidden—his own position, and even his name.

More than anything else in Pierre's story, the captain was impressed by the fact that Pierre was very rich, had two mansions in Moscow, and that he had abandoned everything and not left the city, but remained there concealing his name and station.

When it was late at night they went out together into the street. The night was warm and light. To the left of the house on Pokrovka, a fire glowed—the first of those that were beginning in Moscow. To the right and high up in the sky hung the sickle of the waning moon, and opposite it hung that bright comet which was connected in Pierre's heart with his love. At the gate stood Gerasim, the cook, and two Frenchmen. Their laughter and their mutually incomprehensible remarks in two languages could be heard. They were looking at the glow in the town.
There was nothing frightening about the one small, distant fire in the immense city.

Gazing at the high starry sky, at the moon, at the comet, and at the glow from the fire, Pierre felt a rush of joyful emotion. "There now, how good it is, what more does one need?" thought he. And suddenly, remembering his plan, he grew dizzy and felt so faint that he leaned against the fence to keep from falling.
Without taking leave of his new friend, Pierre left the gate with unsteady steps and, returning to his room, lay down on the sofa and immediately fell asleep.
